mainEntity.name: What is a budget planner?

acceptedAnswer.text: A budget planner is a tool that helps you compare monthly income with spending so you can see what is left for savings, investing, or debt payoff.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate my monthly budget?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add up your monthly income, list your regular and flexible expenses, then subtract total expenses from total income to find your surplus or deficit.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between fixed and variable expenses?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fixed expenses tend to stay similar each month, such as rent or insurance. Variable expenses change more often, such as groceries, dining out, or entertainment.

mainEntity.name: What is a good monthly savings rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: A good savings rate depends on your goals and stage of life, but even small positive monthly surpluses can build momentum over time.

mainEntity.name: Can I use this budget planner for debt payoff planning?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Your monthly surplus can help you estimate how much extra room you may have for debt payments once your core expenses are covered.

mainEntity.name: Can I use this budget planner before investing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Budgeting first gives you a clearer view of the cash flow you may be able to direct toward investing while keeping your bills and savings goals on track.

mainEntity.name: What is compound interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compound interest means your money can earn growth on both the amount you invest and the returns already earned, which can make long-term growth accelerate over time.

mainEntity.name: How often should I contribute?

acceptedAnswer.text: Whatever schedule you can maintain consistently is usually best. Monthly, biweekly, or annual contributions can all work, but recurring contributions generally increase long-term compound growth.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator include inflation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. You can view inflation-adjusted results to translate future balances into today's purchasing-power terms.

mainEntity.name: How do fees affect long-term growth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fees reduce the return that stays invested, which lowers the amount that compounds for you over time and can create a meaningful long-term drag on ending value.

mainEntity.name: Does this compound interest calculator include contributions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. You can model recurring monthly, biweekly, or annual contributions, an optional annual increase in contributions, and one future lump-sum addition.

mainEntity.name: Why adjust for inflation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Inflation adjustment helps translate future dollars into today's purchasing-power terms so you can compare nominal compound growth with real-world spending value.

mainEntity.name: What is an effective hourly rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: An effective hourly rate is your adjusted annual earnings divided by your full-year standard contract hours. It helps you compare offers more fairly than looking only at the advertised hourly rate.

mainEntity.name: Does unpaid vacation reduce hourly rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Unpaid vacation lowers the number of paid weeks in the year, which reduces annual earnings and lowers the practical value of the advertised rate.

mainEntity.name: How do self-paid benefits affect compensation?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you pay for your own health, dental, disability, or insurance coverage, those costs reduce your real compensation and should be included when comparing contract offers.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator include taxes?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. This tool is for pre-tax compensation planning and offer comparison. Taxes, incorporation costs, reimbursable expenses, and province-specific rules are not included.

acceptedAnswer.text: Minimum payments are often low enough that a meaningful share goes toward interest instead of principal. That slows progress and can stretch repayment over many years.

mainEntity.name: Does paying extra each month really save interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes. A higher payment lowers the balance faster, which reduces future interest charges and shortens the payoff timeline.

mainEntity.name: What happens if my payment is too low?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your payment does not cover the interest added each month, the balance may not shrink much and can even keep growing. This calculator flags that as a low-payment warning.

mainEntity.name: What is a debt-to-income ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: A debt-to-income ratio compares your required monthly debt payments with your gross monthly income before tax. It is a quick way to see how much of your monthly income is already spoken for.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate DTI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add up the monthly payments you want counted, then divide that total by your gross monthly income. Back-end DTI includes debt plus housing. Front-end DTI looks only at housing cost.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between front-end and back-end DTI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Front-end DTI looks only at housing cost. Back-end DTI adds housing to your other monthly debt payments. For most people, back-end DTI is the more useful planning number.

mainEntity.name: What is considered a good debt-to-income ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Lower is usually better because it leaves more room in your budget. Many people use broad planning ranges like under 36 percent for a stronger position, 36 to 43 percent for a workable range, and above 43 percent for more pressure. These are guidelines only, not lender promises.

mainEntity.name: Does DTI include rent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it can. If you want a snapshot of your current obligations, rent can be part of your housing cost. If you are planning for a future mortgage, you may want to test that proposed payment instead.

mainEntity.name: Do credit card balances or minimum payments count?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually the monthly payment matters more than the full balance. For credit cards, the most practical number to use is the required minimum monthly payment.

mainEntity.name: Does DTI include utilities or groceries?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually no. DTI planning is mostly about required debt and housing payments, not regular living costs like groceries or entertainment. Some people include heating in housing assumptions, which is why this calculator gives you that option.

mainEntity.name: Can I qualify for a mortgage with a high DTI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Possibly, but a higher DTI can make approval harder and leave less room for unexpected costs. Mortgage decisions depend on more than one number, so this tool is best used for planning, not prediction.

mainEntity.name: How can I lower my debt-to-income ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: The usual ways are to lower monthly debt payments, increase gross income, or choose a lower housing payment. Even a small change to one loan or payment can improve the result.

mainEntity.name: Is this DTI calculator accurate?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is accurate for the numbers you enter, but it is still a planning estimate. Real lenders may count debts differently or apply extra rules that are not built into a general calculator.

acceptedAnswer.text: Three months can be a reasonable starting point if your income is stable and your expenses are predictable, but some households prefer a larger cushion.

mainEntity.name: What expenses should I include?

acceptedAnswer.text: Focus on essentials such as housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, insurance, minimum debt payments, and core household costs.

mainEntity.name: What is FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: FIRE stands for Financial Independence, Retire Early. The core idea is simple: build enough invested assets that work becomes optional because your portfolio can help cover your annual spending.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate your FIRE number?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your FIRE number starts with annual spending, adjusted for any reliable passive income you expect in retirement. A common shortcut is dividing net spending by your withdrawal rate, or multiplying annual spending by a withdrawal multiple such as 25x.

mainEntity.name: What is a good savings rate for FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no perfect number, but higher savings rates usually shorten the timeline because they increase contributions and often reflect lower spending. Even moderate increases can materially change your projection.

mainEntity.name: How much do I need to retire early?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends more on what you spend than on a headline target. Someone spending $50,000 per year needs a very different portfolio than someone spending $100,000 per year.

mainEntity.name: Does the 4% rule work in Canada?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 4% rule is a rough planning guideline, not a guarantee. Canadian taxes, asset mix, sequence risk, inflation, and account structure all affect how safe a withdrawal plan may be.

mainEntity.name: Can TFSA and RRSP be used for FIRE?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Both can be part of a FIRE plan. TFSAs provide tax-free withdrawals, while RRSPs can reduce taxes during high-earning years and still be useful later with thoughtful withdrawal planning.

mainEntity.name: What does this house affordability calculator estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: It estimates an affordable home price, a monthly housing payment, your front-end housing ratio, your back-end debt ratio, and whether the scenario appears conservative, comfortable, or stretched.

mainEntity.name: How is affordability different from mortgage pre-approval?

acceptedAnswer.text: Affordability is a planning estimate based on common income and debt guidelines. A mortgage pre-approval is a lender decision based on your credit profile, documents, debt details, and current lending rules.

mainEntity.name: Should I include property taxes, insurance, and condo fees?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. These costs are part of the real monthly cost of owning a home, so leaving them out can make a home look more affordable than it actually is.

mainEntity.name: Does a bigger down payment increase affordability?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes. A larger down payment lowers the amount you need to borrow, which can reduce the monthly mortgage payment and increase the home price you can afford.

mainEntity.name: What is a good housing ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many affordability guidelines look for housing costs to stay near or below about 28% to 32% of gross income, with total debt payments often kept near or below about 36% to 40%.

mainEntity.name: Why might the calculator say my budget is stretched?

acceptedAnswer.text: A stretched result usually means the monthly housing cost, your debt payments, or both are pushing beyond common affordability thresholds. That can leave less room for maintenance, utilities, savings, and unexpected expenses.

mainEntity.name: Can I use this calculator to compare buying with renting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. It is a helpful starting point for understanding what monthly ownership may look like before comparing it to your current rent and other housing options.

Source: CFPB DTI explainer Utilities count HUD and CMHC affordability frameworks treat utilities or heating as part of housing affordability, which is why this tool includes them. Source: HUD utility allowance guidance · CMHC debt service calculator How to read the result Affordability is about margin, not just approval The best number is not always the highest number. A workable budget should still leave room for repairs, moving costs, utilities, savings, and life outside the mortgage. Conservative Your debt load and fixed ownership costs leave more breathing room. This usually means more flexibility for maintenance, savings, and future rate changes. Comfortable The estimate broadly fits common affordability guidelines, but it is still worth comparing the payment with your own budget habits and other near-term goals. Stretched Debt payments or fixed housing costs are taking up a larger share of income. That can make the payment more sensitive to rate changes, repairs, or income interruptions. FAQ Common questions about house affordability These quick answers are meant to help you use the calculator more confidently. What does this house affordability calculator estimate? It estimates an affordable home price, a monthly housing payment, your front-end housing ratio, your back-end debt ratio, and whether the scenario appears conservative, comfortable, or stretched. How is affordability different from mortgage pre-approval? Affordability is a planning estimate based on common income and debt guidelines. A mortgage pre-approval is a lender decision based on your credit profile, documents, debt details, and current lending rules. Why do monthly debt payments matter so much? Car loans, student loans, credit cards, and other required monthly debt payments reduce how much room you have for a mortgage payment. That is why they directly affect the back-end affordability ratio. Should I include property taxes, insurance, and condo fees? Yes. These costs are part of the real monthly cost of owning a home, so leaving them out can make a home look more affordable than it actually is. Does a bigger down payment increase affordability? Usually yes. A larger down payment lowers the amount you need to borrow, which can reduce the monthly mortgage payment and increase the home price you can afford. What is a good housing ratio? Many affordability guidelines look for housing costs to stay near or below about 28% to 32% of gross income, with total debt payments often kept near or below about 36% to 40%. Exact limits vary by lender and borrower. Why might the calculator say my budget is stretched? A stretched result usually means the monthly housing cost, your debt payments, or both are pushing beyond common affordability thresholds. That can leave less room for maintenance, utilities, savings, and unexpected expenses. Can I use this calculator to compare buying with renting? Yes. It is a helpful starting point for understanding what monthly ownership may look like before comparing it to your current rent and other housing options. mainEntity.name: What is an investment fee?

acceptedAnswer.text: An investment fee is a cost charged for managing or administering an investment product. In many funds, that cost is expressed as an MER and reduces the return that stays invested.

mainEntity.name: What is MER?

acceptedAnswer.text: MER stands for management expense ratio. It is usually shown as an annual percentage and represents ongoing fund costs that come out of the investment rather than being billed separately.

mainEntity.name: How much do investment fees cost over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: The long-term cost depends on your balance, contributions, time horizon, returns, and fee level. Even a seemingly small annual difference can produce a large ending-wealth gap after decades of compounding.

mainEntity.name: Do low-fee ETFs really make a difference?

acceptedAnswer.text: They can. Lower fees do not guarantee a better investment outcome, but they usually mean you keep more of the gross return if all else is equal.

mainEntity.name: How do fees affect retirement savings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fees lower the return that remains in your portfolio. Over long retirement-saving timelines, that can reduce the amount available for future spending or withdrawals.

mainEntity.name: Why do fees matter so much over 20 to 30 years?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the drag repeats every year. A lower balance early on means less capital available to compound later, so the gap can widen more than many investors expect.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between an ETF fee and a mutual fund fee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both can charge ongoing costs, but ETFs often have lower MERs than traditional mutual funds. The exact difference depends on the specific product, provider, and what is included in the fee.

pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Cash flow planning Budgeting & cash flow From a Monthly Budget to a Cash Flow Plan: Know What’s Available Before Payday By SimpleKit · Published October 2, 2026 · 7 minute read Your monthly budget says you have money left over. Your bank account feels tight a week before payday. Both can be true: the total for the month and the timing of each payment answer different questions. A cash flow plan puts income and outgoing payments on a calendar. It helps you see the lowest projected balance before your next payday, so you can distinguish money you hold from money you can still allocate. Build your monthly budget In this guide Budget versus cash flow A worked payday example Build your cash flow plan Avoid counting credit card spending twice Keep the plan current When Capehelm can help Common questions What is the difference between a budget and a cash flow plan? A monthly budget assigns your income to expenses, savings and debt repayment. A cash flow plan tracks when money actually enters or leaves an account. You need both the amount and the date to know whether a payment is covered. Your budget answers “Can we afford our month?” For example, $6,000 of take-home income minus $5,400 of planned spending, saving and debt payments leaves $600 unallocated. That is a useful monthly starting point. Your forecast answers “Can this account cover Tuesday?” If rent, insurance and a credit card payment land before your next deposit, the account can run short even when the month as a whole balances. If you have not built the monthly picture yet, start with our monthly budgeting guide and the free Budget Planner . Then add payment dates to the plan. Example: a $2,400 balance with only $150 of room Suppose you have $2,400 available in your chequing account on the 8th, after allowing for pending transactions. Your next $3,000 pay deposit is expected on the 15th. These are fictional Canadian-dollar amounts; they are an illustration, not spending targets. Projected account balance before payday Date Item Change Balance 8th Opening available balance — $2,400 9th Housing payment −$1,100 $1,300 11th Credit card payment −$500 $800 12th Insurance −$150 $650 14th Groceries and transport paid from chequing −$200 $450 15th Pay deposit +$3,000 $3,450 The lowest projected balance before payday is $450 . If you want to keep a $300 operating buffer, the extra room in this example is $150 : $450 minus $300. An additional $250 purchase paid from chequing before payday would bring the projected low to $200, below your chosen buffer. Looking only at today’s $2,400 balance would miss that pressure. Planning estimate: lowest projected balance during the period − chosen operating buffer = potential extra room. A negative result indicates a gap to resolve. The estimate depends on complete entries and correct dates; it is not a guarantee that money is safe to spend. Check the order of same-day deposits and withdrawals. A payday deposit should not be assumed to cover an earlier withdrawal until the money is actually available. How to turn your budget into a cash flow plan 1. Start with the money available now Use the account you pay bills from. Account for pending debits and payments that have not cleared. Do not subtract a pending payment again if the balance you use already reflects it. An overdraft limit or available credit is borrowing capacity, not income. Keep accounts separate when necessary. Money in savings does not cover a chequing withdrawal until you plan and complete the transfer. A transfer between your own accounts changes each account’s balance without creating new household income. 2. Enter actual paydays Put the expected net deposit on each date it should become available. Semi-monthly pay is normally twice each month; biweekly pay is every two weeks. With 26 equal biweekly payments, the annual amount divided by 12 is useful for a monthly budget, but it does not tell you which dates the deposits arrive. For irregular income, separate confirmed receipts from uncertain estimates. A possible invoice payment or reimbursement should not be treated as cash already available. 3. Schedule bills, debt payments and transfers Add rent or mortgage payments, utilities, insurance, subscriptions, childcare, loan payments, card payments and planned savings transfers. Use the expected account withdrawal date, which may differ from the statement date or bill due date. 4. Allow for everyday spending Reserve a realistic amount for food, transport and other essentials before the next pay deposit. Use recent transactions to improve the estimate. Include purchases already committed, such as a booked appointment, even if they have not appeared in your account. 5. Choose a buffer and find the low point An operating buffer is money you intend to leave in the bill-paying account to absorb small timing changes. Its size depends on your obligations and uncertainty. The $300 in our example is illustrative. A separate emergency fund serves a different purpose: unexpected larger costs or an interruption in income. Read the running balance for every date, not just the final total. If the plan falls below your buffer, consider reducing optional spending, rescheduling a voluntary transfer, or asking a provider whether a payment date can change. Confirm any agreed change before relying on it. If the monthly budget itself is negative, shifting dates alone will not fix the underlying gap. Credit card payments: avoid counting the same spending twice A card purchase and the later payment affect different parts of your plan. If you buy $100 of groceries on a credit card, the purchase belongs in your grocery spending category. Paying that $100 from chequing later reduces your cash balance and card debt; it is not a second grocery purchase. For your spending budget: record the original purchase in its category. For your chequing forecast: schedule the payment when cash will leave the account. For future planning: reserve for new card purchases that will need payment beyond your current forecast window. Payments toward older carried debt still need a planned allocation, and interest and fees are separate costs. A forecast can look comfortable before a large card payment just outside the window. Check the next statement payment as well as the next payday. For a carried balance, explore the Credit Card Interest Calculator or Debt Payoff Calculator . A short weekly review keeps the forecast useful Once a week, and after a material change, compare the plan with your actual account balances. Mark cleared payments, correct unexpected amounts, confirm upcoming income, and review the lowest balance for the next one or two weeks. Ask: What must be paid before payday? What everyday spending is still needed? Does the balance dip below our buffer? Is a larger payment approaching just beyond this window? Extend the review when the next payday, an annual bill or a major card payment sits outside the period. For annual expenses, a monthly savings allocation helps you prepare, but the full payment still needs a date in your forecast. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada recommends comparing actual spending with your budget and updating the figures when circumstances change. That habit supports a useful forecast too. See its guide to making a budget . When to move from a calculator to Capehelm SimpleKit is a useful place to build a budget and explore individual decisions. You can maintain the dated cash flow plan described here in a spreadsheet or notebook. If you want a recurring workflow on your Mac, Capehelm’s 14-day cash flow forecast brings upcoming income, expenses, recurring commitments and credit card payments into a projected balance view. Capehelm also supports local CSV statement imports, transaction categorization and budgeting. Those features can help you connect what actually happened with what you expect next. Imports and planned entries need to stay current; a forecast based on old balances or missing payments can mislead you. SimpleKit and Capehelm are created by the same developer. Capehelm is a paid macOS app and an optional next step; you can use this method and SimpleKit’s free Budget Planner without it. Start with the free Budget Planner Explore Capehelm for Mac Cash flow planning questions Why am I short before payday if my budget balances? Your monthly income may cover your monthly commitments, but several payments can fall before the income arrives. Missing expenses or underestimated spending can also cause a gap. A dated running balance helps distinguish a timing problem from a budget shortfall. How much of my bank balance is available to spend? Start with available cash, include confirmed incoming money and all expected outgoing payments, and find the lowest projected balance in the period. Subtract your operating buffer, then check obligations beyond that period. Do not treat the current balance alone as a spending allowance. Should I use a monthly budget or a payday budget? Use a monthly budget for your overall allocation and a payday plan for timing. Together they show whether the month is affordable and whether each payment can be covered when it leaves your account. Do I need an app to make a cash flow plan? No. A notebook or spreadsheet with dates, deposits, withdrawals and a running balance can work. Software can make repeated updates more convenient, but the quality of the plan still depends on the information you enter. Give the monthly plan a calendar Build your budget, map the next paydays and payments, then check the lowest projected balance. That turns “we should have money left this month” into a clearer picture of what your money needs to cover next. Open the SimpleKit Budget Planner Educational information. Fees work in the opposite direction: money removed from the portfolio no longer has the same opportunity to compound. What drives compound growth Time gives compounding room to work The longer money remains invested, the more periods there are for returns to build on earlier returns. That is why starting earlier can matter even when contributions are modest. Contributions often matter more than tiny return tweaks A consistent savings habit adds fresh capital to the compounding base. For many plans, increasing contributions is more controllable than trying to predict a slightly higher return. Returns are assumptions, not promises A smooth annual growth rate is useful for modelling but real markets fluctuate. Test lower and higher return scenarios rather than treating one forecast as certain. Why ongoing fees deserve attention A fee reduces the return that stays invested If two otherwise identical investments earn the same gross return, the one with lower ongoing costs leaves more money in the account to compound. Small annual differences accumulate A fee that looks small in one year can create a much larger ending-value gap after decades because the lost dollars also lose future growth. Cost is not the only investment criterion Risk, diversification, taxes, suitability, trading behaviour, and the investment itself still matter. Fees are one important variable, not a complete investment decision. Put the idea into your own numbers. pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Credit Card Interest and Payoff SimpleKit Learn Credit Card Interest and Payoff Credit cards are flexible, but carrying a balance can make small purchases expensive over time. The key variables are the balance, annual interest rate, required payment, and how much extra you can consistently send to principal. Why revolving credit can linger Interest keeps working against the balance When you carry a balance, interest adds borrowing cost while your payment is trying to reduce principal. A higher rate leaves less of each payment available to shrink the debt. Minimum payments are designed to keep the account current A minimum payment is not a payoff strategy. Depending on the balance and card terms, paying only the minimum can stretch repayment over a long period. Extra payments attack principal sooner Paying more than the required amount reduces the balance earlier, which reduces the amount on which future interest is charged. New purchases can erase progress A payoff forecast assumes the balance follows the model. Continuing to add purchases can extend the timeline even when every scheduled payment is made. Use the payoff estimate as a decision tool Compare payment levels Testing several monthly payments shows how much time and interest a manageable increase could save. Compare expensive debts together If you have multiple balances, the interest rate and minimum payment on each debt help determine which one deserves extra cash first. Be careful with consolidation A lower-rate loan can reduce interest, but only if fees, term length, and new borrowing do not erase the benefit. Put the idea into your own numbers. pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Debt Snowball vs Avalanche SimpleKit Learn Debt Snowball vs Avalanche The debt snowball and debt avalanche use the same basic idea: keep making minimum payments on every debt and direct extra cash to one balance at a time. The difference is which balance gets attacked first. Two payoff orders, two different advantages Debt avalanche: highest rate first The avalanche directs extra money to the debt with the highest interest rate. If payments and timing are otherwise identical, this generally minimizes interest cost. Debt snowball: smallest balance first The snowball targets the smallest balance regardless of rate. Clearing an account sooner can create visible progress and free one minimum payment to roll into the next debt. Minimum payments continue everywhere else Both methods depend on keeping every account current while concentrating extra payments. Missing required payments can create fees, credit damage, or higher borrowing costs. The best plan is one you can sustain The avalanche can be mathematically cheaper, but a method that causes you to quit is not useful. Compare the dollar difference and decide whether faster psychological wins are worth any extra interest. Make the payoff plan stronger Stop adding expensive balances A payoff schedule cannot make progress if new high-interest borrowing replaces the principal you just repaid. Use windfalls deliberately Tax refunds, bonuses, and other irregular cash can shorten the payoff period dramatically when they go directly to principal. Protect a small cash buffer Without any emergency cash, a routine surprise can push spending straight back onto credit. Debt payoff and resilience need to work together. pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Emergency Funds and Savings Goals SimpleKit Learn Emergency Funds and Savings Goals Emergency savings and planned savings solve different problems. An emergency fund protects against unexpected financial shocks; a savings goal turns a known future expense into a manageable monthly target. Build the emergency fund around the risks you actually face Start with essential expenses Housing, food, utilities, transportation, insurance, and minimum debt payments are a more useful base than total lifestyle spending when estimating how long a cash reserve could last. Job stability changes the target A household with two stable incomes may need a different buffer than a single-income household, contractor, or worker in a volatile industry. There is no universal number of months that fits everyone. Keep true emergencies liquid Emergency money is most useful when it can be accessed quickly without selling a volatile investment at a bad time or borrowing at a high interest rate. Do not use the emergency fund for predictable bills Annual insurance, holidays, vehicle maintenance, and travel are irregular but foreseeable. Separate sinking funds keep those costs from repeatedly draining the emergency reserve. Turn a known goal into a monthly number Define the amount and date A goal becomes actionable when it has a target amount and time horizon. Divide the remaining amount by the months available for a simple starting contribution. Account for existing savings Money already set aside reduces the remaining gap. Interest or investment growth may help, but short timelines usually leave less room to rely on uncertain returns. Prioritize competing goals Emergency reserves, high-interest debt, retirement contributions, and near-term purchases can compete for the same cash. A budget makes those tradeoffs visible. pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Loan Payments and Amortization SimpleKit Learn Loan Payments and Amortization A loan payment is the result of several moving parts: the amount borrowed, interest rate, repayment period, and payment schedule. Amortization shows how those payments gradually shift from interest toward principal. Understand what drives the payment Principal is the amount being repaid A larger starting balance generally means a larger payment or a longer repayment period when the rate is unchanged. Interest is the price of borrowing A higher interest rate raises the borrowing cost and usually the required payment. The exact result depends on how the loan compounds and how often payments are made. Longer amortization lowers the payment but raises total interest Stretching repayment over more periods can make each payment easier to carry while keeping the balance outstanding—and accruing interest—for longer. Extra payments shorten the schedule When an extra payment goes to principal without a penalty, future interest is calculated on a smaller balance and the payoff date can move forward. Read an amortization schedule Interest and principal change over time With a typical level-payment loan, early payments contain more interest because the balance is larger. As principal falls, more of the same payment can go toward principal. Outstanding balance is the key checkpoint The balance after each payment shows how quickly the debt is actually disappearing and makes different repayment strategies easier to compare. Check your actual contract Fees, variable rates, payment rules, prepayment restrictions, and compounding conventions can make a real loan differ from a general calculator. pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Monthly Budgeting and Cash Flow SimpleKit Learn Monthly Budgeting and Cash Flow A useful budget is not a punishment or a perfect forecast. It is a simple model of where take-home pay needs to go, what is already committed, and how much room remains for savings, debt repayment, and irregular expenses. Build the budget in the right order Start with take-home pay Gross salary is useful for tax planning, but monthly spending decisions happen with net income. Use a realistic after-tax figure as the amount available to allocate. Separate fixed from flexible costs Housing, insurance, debt payments, and subscriptions behave differently from groceries, dining, fuel, and discretionary spending. Separating them makes the budget easier to adjust. Treat savings as a planned use of cash Emergency savings, retirement contributions, and short-term goals are easier to sustain when they appear in the plan before leftover money disappears. Leave room for irregular costs Annual fees, vehicle repairs, gifts, school costs, and travel can make a balanced month look misleading. A sinking-fund line can spread those costs across the year. Use the budget as a feedback loop Compare plan with actual spending The first version is only a hypothesis. Review where actual spending differs and adjust the assumptions rather than forcing every month to look identical. Use surplus intentionally A monthly surplus can fund debt payoff, emergency savings, investing, or a near-term goal. Giving it a purpose makes progress visible. Watch fixed-cost creep Recurring obligations are harder to reverse than one-time spending. When fixed costs grow, the household loses flexibility even if income is unchanged. Plan what is available before payday Give your monthly budget a calendar of income and payments. Build a cash flow plan with a worked example Put the idea into your own numbers. pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Mortgage Affordability in Canada SimpleKit Learn Mortgage Affordability in Canada Mortgage affordability is not just a house-price question. It is a relationship between income, existing debt, down payment, mortgage terms, taxes, heating costs, and the rate a lender uses to test whether the payment is manageable. Start with the payment, then widen the view Income sets the ceiling Gross household income is the starting point for most affordability screens. A higher income can support a larger payment, but existing debt and housing costs reduce the room available. Debt service ratios matter Canadian mortgage underwriting commonly uses Gross Debt Service (GDS) for housing costs and Total Debt Service (TDS) after adding other debt obligations. These are lender qualification tools, not household comfort targets. The stress test changes the qualifying payment For many mortgages, qualification uses a rate higher than the contract rate. That means the payment you can afford in day-to-day cash flow may be larger than the payment a lender will qualify. Ownership costs extend beyond principal and interest Property tax, heating, condo fees, insurance, maintenance, and repairs do not disappear because the mortgage payment fits. A realistic home budget should leave room for those costs too. Use three numbers instead of one A comfortable housing budget This is the payment and ownership cost that fits your real monthly cash flow while preserving room for savings, debt repayment, and surprises. A lender-style screening limit This uses income and debt-service rules to estimate where borrowing may become harder. It is useful context, but it is not a pre-approval. The purchase price those assumptions imply Down payment and mortgage rate translate the monthly budget into a rough home-price range. Changing either can move the result materially. A realistic budget separates principal, interest, recurring ownership expenses, and irregular costs. Break the payment into what it actually does Principal builds equity The principal portion reduces the loan balance. It is a transfer from cash into home equity rather than a pure expense. Interest is the cost of borrowing Interest does not build equity. Early in an amortization schedule, a larger share of each payment may go to interest. Payment frequency changes timing more than economics Weekly, biweekly, and monthly schedules can change when money leaves your account. Accelerated schedules can also increase the annual amount paid and shorten amortization when the total annual payment is higher. Add the ownership costs that sit outside the mortgage Property tax and insurance These are recurring costs of ownership and should be budgeted alongside the mortgage, not treated as occasional extras. Maintenance and repairs Roofing, appliances, plumbing, exterior work, and routine upkeep arrive unevenly. A monthly reserve can make those costs less disruptive. Utilities and condo fees Heating, electricity, water, and condo fees can materially change the monthly cost of a property even when the mortgage is unchanged. Buying and selling costs Legal fees, inspections, moving costs, land-transfer taxes where applicable, commissions, and other transaction costs matter most when the holding period is short. pages.description: Learn how to compare extra mortgage payments with investing by weighing guaranteed interest savings, expected returns, taxes, risk, liquidity, and prepayment rules.
pages.bodyText: SimpleKit SimpleKit Free planning tools with clearer next steps Home Tools Learn About Support Home / Learn / Mortgage Prepayment vs Investing SimpleKit Learn Mortgage Prepayment vs Investing Paying down a mortgage and investing can both strengthen a household balance sheet, but they create different kinds of value. The cleanest comparison separates the guaranteed return from avoided mortgage interest from the uncertain after-tax return of investing. What extra mortgage payments give you A guaranteed interest saving An extra principal payment reduces future interest at the mortgage rate. Unlike an investment return, the interest avoided is known once the payment is made. Lower debt and fixed obligations A smaller balance can reduce renewal risk and move the debt-free date forward. That can matter even when investing has a higher expected return. Less liquidity Money paid into the mortgage is tied up in home equity. Accessing it later may require refinancing, a line of credit, or selling the property. What investing gives you Higher expected return, but with uncertainty Diversified investments may outperform the mortgage rate over long periods, but returns are not guaranteed and market declines can occur at inconvenient times. Tax treatment can change the comparison A TFSA can shelter future investment growth from tax, while RRSP contributions can create a deduction now and taxable withdrawals later. Taxable accounts add another layer of tax drag. Liquidity and flexibility Invested assets are generally easier to redirect toward another goal than home equity, although market value can be lower when you need the money. A useful decision rule Compare after-tax expected return with the mortgage rate The mortgage rate is a useful hurdle because prepaying avoids that interest with certainty. Investing needs to beat the hurdle after fees and taxes to create a financial advantage. Then include risk and preference If the numbers are close, the better choice may come down to your tolerance for debt, need for liquidity, investment horizon, and comfort with volatility. A useful comparison looks beyond the monthly rent and mortgage payment to the full cash-flow and wealth-building tradeoff over the time you expect to stay. Compare the full cost of each path Rent is more than a monthly cheque Rent can rise over time, but renters usually avoid property tax, major repairs, and many transaction costs. The key question is what happens to the cash that is not tied up in ownership. Buying is more than the mortgage payment Interest, property tax, maintenance, insurance, transaction costs, and the opportunity cost of the down payment all matter. Principal repayment builds equity, but interest and many ownership costs do not. Time horizon can dominate the answer Buying has meaningful upfront and exit costs. A short stay can make those costs harder to recover, while a longer stay gives home equity and appreciation more time to matter. Investing the difference keeps the comparison fair If renting costs less each month or requires less upfront cash, the comparison should model what happens if that difference is invested rather than simply spent. Treat the result as a sensitivity test Home appreciation is uncertain Small changes in assumed appreciation can materially change the long-run result. Test a range rather than relying on one optimistic number. Investment returns are uncertain too A higher assumed market return can favour renting if the renter invests the difference, but actual returns vary and arrive unevenly. Lifestyle still matters Control over the property, mobility, school plans, renovation preferences, and tolerance for maintenance can matter as much as the spreadsheet result. mainEntity.name: How is a loan payment calculated?

acceptedAnswer.text: The payment is based on the loan balance, interest rate, term length, payment frequency, and compounding assumptions. With interest-bearing loans, each payment covers accrued interest plus some principal.

mainEntity.name: What is amortization?

acceptedAnswer.text: Amortization is the schedule that shows how each payment is divided between interest and principal until the balance reaches zero.

mainEntity.name: How do extra payments reduce interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Extra payments lower the outstanding balance earlier, which reduces future interest charges and usually shortens the payoff period.

mainEntity.name: Can I save my loan scenarios?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Export all scenarios and calculator settings as a JSON file, then load the same file later to continue working.

mainEntity.name: How do extra mortgage payments help?

acceptedAnswer.text: Extra mortgage payments reduce principal faster, which lowers future interest charges and can shorten the payoff timeline.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between bi-weekly and accelerated bi-weekly payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: A standard bi-weekly payment spreads a monthly-equivalent mortgage payment across 26 periods. An accelerated bi-weekly payment uses half of the standard monthly payment, which usually adds one extra monthly payment over the year.

mainEntity.name: Why show a mortgage term and an amortization period?

acceptedAnswer.text: Amortization is the full payoff timeline used to calculate the required payment. The term is the shorter contract period that helps show how much balance, interest, and principal remain when renewal time arrives.

mainEntity.name: Is it better to pay off a mortgage or invest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither option is always best. Paying down a mortgage gives a guaranteed return equal to the interest you avoid. Investing may produce a better long-term result, but only if real returns, taxes, and fees work in your favour.

mainEntity.name: What mortgage rate changes the answer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Higher mortgage rates usually make prepayments more attractive because the guaranteed savings become more valuable. Lower mortgage rates give investing more room to outperform, especially over longer periods.

mainEntity.name: Should I invest instead of making extra mortgage payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: That can make sense when you have a long horizon, can tolerate volatility, and have access to tax-efficient accounts like a TFSA or RRSP. It may matter less if you want certainty or need to be debt-free sooner.

mainEntity.name: How does risk affect the decision?

acceptedAnswer.text: Risk changes both the path and the experience. A projected 6% market return may not arrive smoothly, while mortgage savings are immediate and predictable. Your comfort with swings in account value matters.

mainEntity.name: Should I use my TFSA before paying off my mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A TFSA can improve investing efficiency because gains can compound without ongoing tax drag. That may tilt the comparison toward investing, but your mortgage rate, renewal risk, and debt comfort still matter.

mainEntity.name: What if I care more about peace of mind than maximum expected return?

acceptedAnswer.text: That is a valid reason to favour mortgage prepayments. Personal finance is not just about maximizing a spreadsheet result. Reducing fixed obligations can make a household feel safer and more flexible.

mainEntity.name: What is net worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Net worth is the value of what you own minus what you owe. It combines cash, investments, real estate, pensions, and other assets, then subtracts debts such as mortgages, loans, and credit cards.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate net worth in Canada?

acceptedAnswer.text: In Canada, net worth is calculated by adding assets such as cash, TFSAs, RRSPs, FHSAs, pensions, real estate, and vehicles, then subtracting liabilities such as mortgages, HELOCs, loans, and other debts.

mainEntity.name: Should you include your house in net worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, many people include their home because home equity is part of their balance sheet. The important step is to include both the property value and the related mortgage or HELOC.

mainEntity.name: Is pension included in net worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: A pension can be included if you use a reasonable estimate for its present value. If you do not have a clear estimate, you can leave it blank and review it later.

mainEntity.name: What is a good net worth by age?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single good net worth number by age because income, housing costs, pensions, family size, and when you started saving all matter. The more useful question is whether your net worth is moving in the right direction over time.

mainEntity.name: How does net worth connect to retirement planning?

acceptedAnswer.text: Net worth shows the resources you may be able to draw on later, but retirement readiness also depends on retirement income sources, spending needs, taxes, and timing decisions such as CPP or RRSP withdrawals.

Keep it plain: assets are what you own, liabilities are what you owe, and your net worth is the difference. Assets Assets include cash, investments, pensions, real estate, vehicles, business value, and anything else with meaningful resale or financial value. Liabilities Liabilities include mortgages, HELOCs, lines of credit, student loans, car loans, credit cards, and other debts that reduce your balance sheet. Why home equity matters Your home can be one of your biggest assets. Equity is what is left after subtracting the mortgage and any related borrowing such as a HELOC. Formula Net Worth = Total Assets - Total Liabilities Pensions can be estimated Defined benefit pensions are not always easy to value, so an estimate is acceptable. What is net worth? Net worth is a snapshot of your finances at a point in time. It helps you see whether your assets are growing faster than your debts and whether your household is building long-term financial strength. How do you calculate net worth in Canada? Add your cash, TFSA, RRSP, FHSA, non-registered investments, pensions, property, vehicles, and other assets. Then subtract mortgages, HELOCs, loans, credit cards, and other debts. Should you include your house in net worth? Usually yes. For many households, home equity is a large part of total net worth. The key is to include both the home value and the remaining mortgage balance. Is pension included in net worth? It can be, especially if you have a pension statement that gives you a commuted value or another estimate. If you are unsure, you can leave it out for now and add it later. What is a good net worth by age? There is no single number that fits everyone. Income, housing costs, pensions, family size, and when you started saving all matter. mainEntity.name: Is it better to rent or buy a home?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your timeline, local housing costs, down payment, expected appreciation, rent increases, and whether you invest the money you do not put into a home. This calculator helps compare those tradeoffs side by side.

mainEntity.name: How does a rent vs buy calculator work?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rent vs buy calculator compares the ongoing cost of renting with the full cost of owning, then estimates how home equity and renter investments may grow over time.

mainEntity.name: Is renting cheaper than a mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes. A mortgage payment alone can look similar to rent, but buying also includes property taxes, insurance, maintenance, fees, closing costs, and selling costs. This calculator compares the full picture.

mainEntity.name: Does renting ever build more wealth than buying?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Renting can come out ahead when home costs are high, your time horizon is short, appreciation is modest, or you consistently invest the money you avoid tying up in the home.

mainEntity.name: What is a break-even year in a rent vs buy comparison?

acceptedAnswer.text: The break-even year is the point when buying catches up to or overtakes renting on projected ending net worth for the selected assumptions.

A rent vs buy calculator compares the long-term financial impact of renting with the full cost of owning, then estimates how home equity and renter investments may grow over time. Why time horizon matters Buying often looks worse over short periods because closing and selling costs are front-loaded. Over longer periods, appreciation and mortgage paydown have more time to help. When buying may make sense Buying can make more sense when you expect to stay put, can handle the upfront costs, and believe the home will build equity faster than renting plus investing. When renting may be financially better Renting can come out ahead when ownership costs are high, your expected stay is shorter, or the renter invests the difference instead of letting that cash sit idle. Why investing the difference matters If renting costs less each month, those savings can compound. In some cases, that investment growth can outweigh the equity built by buying. That is why a home does not automatically beat renting, even when it builds equity. Investing Returns on the renter path matter If renting leaves room to invest consistently and those returns are solid, the renter path can close the gap or pull ahead. mainEntity.name: Is RRSP or TFSA better in Canada?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your current marginal tax rate, your expected retirement tax rate, and whether you reinvest the RRSP refund. Higher current tax rates often improve the RRSP case, while lower current tax rates and flexibility often strengthen the TFSA case.

mainEntity.name: Does an RRSP always beat a TFSA?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. An RRSP can lead when your tax rate is higher today than in retirement, especially if you reinvest the refund. A TFSA can lead when tax rates are similar, when future tax may be higher, or when flexibility matters more.

mainEntity.name: Should I reinvest my RRSP refund?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often yes. Reinvesting the RRSP refund usually makes the RRSP comparison stronger because it preserves the full tax benefit instead of spending it.

mainEntity.name: Does province affect RRSP savings?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Your province or territory affects your estimated current marginal tax rate, which changes the size of the RRSP refund and can shift the comparison.

mainEntity.name: What is take-home pay?

acceptedAnswer.text: Take-home pay is the amount left after payroll deductions come off your gross salary. In this calculator that usually means federal tax, provincial or territorial tax, CPP or QPP, and EI.

mainEntity.name: Why is my take-home pay different in each province?

acceptedAnswer.text: Federal tax applies across Canada, but provincial and territorial income tax systems differ. That changes your estimated deductions and net pay even when the salary stays the same.

mainEntity.name: Does CPP stop during the year?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. If your salary is high enough to reach the annual maximum employee contribution before December, that deduction may stop for the rest of the year.

mainEntity.name: Does EI stop during the year?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. EI also has an annual employee maximum premium, so some workers will see EI stop later in the year if they hit the cap.

mainEntity.name: How do you estimate when CPP and EI are paid up?

acceptedAnswer.text: The calculator assumes steady salary and applies the same monthly earnings pattern across the full year to estimate when each annual maximum would be reached.

mainEntity.name: Is this calculator accurate for Quebec?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is useful for planning, but Quebec payroll treatment can differ in practice. Confirm exact figures with Revenu Quebec, the CRA, or your payroll provider if you need payroll-accurate numbers.

mainEntity.name: Why can my paycheck increase later in the year?

acceptedAnswer.text: If CPP, QPP, or EI reaches its annual maximum during the year, that deduction may stop later pay periods and your net pay can increase even if gross salary stays the same.

mainEntity.name: Can I compare provinces with the same salary?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The comparison feature reuses the same salary and tax year across all provinces and territories so you can explore how location changes estimated take-home pay.
